title: Web Security Vulnerabilities
summary: How SQL injection, XSS, CSRF and SSRF work, what CORS really does, and how parameterized queries, output encoding, SameSite cookies, URL allowlists, secrets management and least privilege prevent them.

questions.prompt: What is **SQL injection**? Show a tiny example of vulnerable code and an input that exploits it, then give the correct fix.
questions.hint: What happens when user input is concatenated into the SQL text and contains a quote?
keyPoints: User input is concatenated into the SQL string, so it can change the query's structure (data treated as code)
Example: email = ' OR '1'='1' -- makes the WHERE clause always true and comments out the rest
Impact: bypass login, read other tables (UNION), modify or delete data
Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements where values are sent separately from SQL text (e.g. WHERE email = $1 with [email])
Defense in depth: least-privilege database user; manual escaping is not the primary fix

questions.hint: What happens if a comment's text is ``?
keyPoints: Stored XSS: author and text are inserted as HTML via innerHTML, so injected tags/attributes like onerror run JavaScript in every viewer's browser
Attacker can act as the victim on the page: make requests with their session, read page data, steal non-HttpOnly cookies, deface or phish
Fix: build elements and set textContent (or use a framework's auto-escaping); never innerHTML with untrusted data
If rich text is needed, sanitize with a vetted library like DOMPurify
Defense in depth: Content-Security-Policy disallowing inline scripts, HttpOnly session cookies

questions.prompt: Your banking site authenticates users with a session cookie and has an endpoint `POST /transfer` taking `to` and `amount` form fields. Explain step by step how a **CSRF** attack against it works, and list the defenses you'd put in place.
questions.hint: The attacker never sees the cookie. Whose browser sends the request, and what does it attach automatically?
keyPoints: Victim is logged in; attacker's page auto-submits a hidden form (or fetch) to bank.example/transfer
The browser automatically attaches the bank's session cookie, so the bank sees a valid authenticated request and executes it
SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies stop the cookie being sent on cross-site POSTs
CSRF tokens: random per-session value required in state-changing requests that the attacker's page cannot read
Check the Origin/Referer header on state-changing requests; never change state with GET
CORS does not prevent this: it limits reading responses, not sending requests

questions.hint: Which addresses can the server reach that an outside attacker can't? Think about `169.254.169.254`.
keyPoints: SSRF: the attacker controls which URL the server fetches, so the server can be aimed at internal targets
Targets: cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 (may expose IAM credentials), localhost services, internal admin panels and databases
Allowlist schemes (https only) and ideally domains; otherwise resolve DNS and reject private, loopback and link-local ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254/16, ::1)
Check the resolved IP and connect to that same IP (DNS rebinding), and re-validate every redirect
Defense in depth: run fetchers in an isolated network/egress proxy, require IMDSv2, limit timeouts and response size

questions.prompt: A developer says: *"We enabled CORS with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` reflecting the request's Origin and `Allow-Credentials: true`, so our API is protected — only browsers that pass CORS can call it."* What's wrong with this statement and configuration?
questions.hint: Who enforces CORS? Does it stop requests or responses? What does reflecting any origin with credentials allow?
keyPoints: Same-origin policy is enforced by browsers; CORS is a server opt-in to relax it, not a server protection
Non-browser clients (curl, scripts) ignore CORS entirely, so it does not authenticate or protect the API
CORS controls whether page JavaScript can read the response; the request itself can still be sent
Reflecting any Origin with credentials allowed lets any website read logged-in users' data from the API
Fix: allowlist specific trusted origins; rely on real authentication/authorization and CSRF defenses for protection

questions.prompt: A developer accidentally pushed a production database password and a cloud API key to a **public** GitHub repo an hour ago. Describe your incident response in order, then design the practices that would prevent this and limit the damage next time.
questions.hint: Is deleting the file enough? Think in order: contain, investigate, fix, prevent. Then apply least privilege.
keyPoints: First rotate/revoke both secrets immediately; deleting the file or commit is not enough because history and scrapers already have it (bots scan within minutes)
Investigate: check cloud audit logs and DB logs for use of the leaked credentials since the push, assess data access, follow incident and disclosure processes
Clean up history (rewrite/purge) only after rotation, as secondary hygiene
Prevention: secrets in a secrets manager or injected env vars, never in code; pre-commit and CI secret scanning; .gitignore for env files
Limit blast radius: least-privilege credentials per service, short-lived credentials (IAM roles), network restrictions on the DB, regular rotation
Blameless post-mortem to fix the process, not the person
